article_title: The Validity of Heart Rate Variability (HRV) in Educational Research and a Synthesis of Recommendations
citation: Hyun Jin Kim, Yuyi Park, Jihyun Lee. (2024). The Validity of Heart Rate Variability (HRV) in Educational Research and a Synthesis of Recommendations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09878-x
title: HRV as a psychophysiological index of autonomic nervous system balance underlying self-regulation
description: The review presents HRV as "a quantitative expression of balance in the functioning of the autonomic nervous system (ANS)", reflecting sympathetic (alertness) versus parasympathetic (relaxation) modulation. Via brain–heart connections — inhibitory GABAergic pathways from prefrontal cortex to amygdala and amygdala regulation of the ANS through hormones and neurotransmitters — HRV indexes physiological, emotional, and cognitive regulation, so high HRV implies balanced ANS allowing flexible, resilient responses, while lower HRV can signal imbalance. Educational studies use it to objectively track learner stress and attention states in real time.
requirements: HRV measurement must account for physiological factors such as cardiac function, respiration rate, age, health status, and medications that influence the signal
constraints: HRV is influenced by a wide range of physiological, emotional, and cognitive factors, so the review warns the information it provides can be easily misconstrued and interpretation difficulties can limit real-world implications
target_learners: learners in educational contexts aged 5 to 65, including primary, secondary, undergraduate, and professional learners
target_learning_goals: understanding learners' emotional and cognitive self-regulation during learning
examples: The review's 48 included studies applied HRV during exams, learning activities, and experiments to capture changes in learner states over time
key_sources: Hyun Jin Kim, Yuyi Park, Jihyun Lee. (2024). The Validity of Heart Rate Variability (HRV) in Educational Research and a Synthesis of Recommendations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09878-x

article_title: Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance
citation: Ackermann, H., Henke, A., Chevalère, J., Yun, H. S., Hafner, V. V., Pinkwart, N., & Lazarides, R. (2025). Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00293-z
title: HRIES: Human-Robot Interaction Evaluation Scale with four anthropomorphism subdimensions
description: The HRIES is a questionnaire assessing the anthropomorphism of a robot using a multicomponent approach based on dehumanization theory and psychosocial theory. As the article states, "It measures the anthropomorphism of a robot using four dimensions: perceived sociability, animacy, agency, and disturbance." Each dimension is a four-item subscale (e.g., sociability: warmth, trustworthy, likable, friendly; disturbance: scary, creepy, uncanny, weird), and the study used it in post-test questionnaires in which students rated the tutor agent. The article reports it has repeatedly shown good psychometric reliability and structural validity.
requirements: Students complete post-test self-report ratings of the robotic agents after interaction, evaluating each agent separately with pictures presented in randomized order
target_learning_goals: perception and evaluation of robotic tutor agents during AI-supported learning
examples: In this study the HRIES was administered after a 60-minute learning session with the emotionally-adaptive ITS Betty's Brain, yielding the sociability, animacy, agency, and disturbance scores used in four separate path models
key_sources: Ackermann, H., Henke, A., Chevalère, J., Yun, H. S., Hafner, V. V., Pinkwart, N., & Lazarides, R. (2025). Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00293-z
